memos.scout:
The strongest honest case is thin, and I don't think it clears the bar. The brief shows the coin is alive, up 6.6% over 30 minutes, with a shallow 0.09% drawdown from its high and 45 buyers versus 14 sellers in the last 15 minutes (net inflow of 12.29 SOL). That is real recent demand.

But the same brief shows the demand is concentrated. Bundle share is 1.0, top-3 share is 1.0, and the top-5 buyers hold 99.8% of early buys, with 1,196 SOL bought in the first two minutes from 18 buyers. That is textbook operator structure, and the 1,307 SOL pool depth against an $11.5M market cap means the price is sensitive to whoever decides to exit. Our $20 ticket would be a tiny fraction of the flow, but the question is whether the operators sell into our buy, and nothing here tells us they won't.

Summing up: the signals that say demand will persist are short-window and driven by the same wallets that dominate the supply. I see no case strong enough to override a roughly break-even base rate after 1.4-5.1% round-trip costs. I recommend skipping.
memos.skeptic:
The most likely loss path is insider distribution. The curve shows bundle_share 1.0 and top3_share 1.0, meaning one operator controlled essentially all early supply, and first_2_min_after_graduation shows 1,196 SOL bought by just 18 buyers, with top5_buyer_share at 0.9977. That is a concentrated bundle, and the operator can sell into any retail demand we provide. The sell_to_buy ratio of 0.0001 means almost no one has sold, which is the signature of a holder who hasn't started exiting yet, not evidence of safety.

Market cap of about $11.5M on a coin 30 minutes old, with only $3.3K of volume in the last 15 minutes, leaves a thin float against a huge valuation. Our $20 ticket plus 1.4-5.1% round-trip costs needs a move just to break even, while a 1.9% recent return is inside that cost band. The name "Institutional Oil Fund" is a creator-chosen lure, not a fundamental signal.

Verdict: skip.
